3y4e01:1317: We have previously shown that harness design has a significant impact on long-running agentic coding. In an earlier experiment, we used an initializer agent to break down product specifications into task lists, and then a coding agent completed tasks one feature at a time, extending context across sessions through artifact handoffs. The broader developer community has also been converging on similar insights, such as the Ralph Wiggum method, which uses hooks or scripts to keep the agent in an iterative loop. But some problems never went away. Once tasks became complex, agents still easily drifted off course over time. In breaking down this problem, we observed two common failure modes. The first is that models tend to lose coherence in long tasks as the context window gradually fills up (see our article on context engineering). Some models also exhibit "context anxiety": when they approach what they believe is their context limit, they start wrapping up prematurely. context reset — that is, completely clearing the context window and starting a new agent, along with a structured handoff document that carries the previous agent's state and next-step plan — can solve both problems at once. This is different from compaction. Compaction summarizes the earlier part of the conversation in place, allowing the same agent to continue based on the shortened history. While compaction preserves continuity, it does not give the agent a truly "clean start," so context anxiety can still exist. The advantage of reset is that it gives the model a genuinely clean context; the cost is that the handoff artifact must carry enough state for the next agent to seamlessly continue. In our early tests, Claude Sonnet 4.5's context anxiety was significant enough that compaction alone could not sustain high-quality long-task performance, so context reset became a key component in the harness design. It did solve the core problem, but it also added orchestration complexity, token overhead, and extra latency to each harness run. The second problem, which we had not specifically addressed before, is self-evaluation. When you ask an agent to evaluate its own output, it tends to confidently praise its own work — even when quality is rather mediocre by human standards. This problem is especially visible in subjective design tasks, because there is no binary verifiable check like software tests. Whether a layout is "exquisite" or "ordinary" is itself a judgment call, and when evaluating its own work, the agent almost always scores in a more positive direction. However, even in tasks with clear verifiable outcomes, agents still show poor judgment that hinders task completion. Separating the "agent that does the work" from the "agent that judges" is a strong lever for solving this problem. This separation alone does not immediately eliminate leniency, because the evaluator itself is still an LLM that tends to go easy on LLM outputs. But tuning an independent evaluator to be "skeptical" is far more realistic than asking the generator to be harsh on itself; once such external feedback exists, the generator has concrete material to iterate on.

f1uapq:676: Over the past few months, I have been working on two interrelated problems: how to get Claude to produce high-quality frontend designs, and how to get it to build complete applications without human intervention. This work originated from our earlier explorations in the frontend design skill and long-running coding agent harness. At that time, my colleagues and I had already made Claude's performance clearly surpass the baseline through prompt engineering and harness design, but both approaches ultimately hit a ceiling. To break through these limits, I began looking for an AI engineering methodology that could apply to two very different domains: one dominated by subjective aesthetics, the other defined by verifiable correctness and usability. Inspired by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), I designed a multi-agent structure composed of a generator and an evaluator. To build an evaluator that could score consistently and also have "taste," the prerequisite was to first establish a set of standards that transform subjective judgments like "Is this design good?" into concrete, scorable items. I then applied these methods to long-running autonomous coding, inheriting two lessons from our earlier harness work: first, break the build task into manageable chunks; second, use structured artifacts to hand off context between sessions. The final result is a three-agent architecture composed of planner, generator, and evaluator, which can produce content-rich full-stack applications in autonomous coding sessions lasting several hours.
